Surah al-Inshiqaq

It is also said: Surah Inshaqqat. It is Meccan without any disagreement, and its verses number twenty-three according to the Basran and Syrian reckonings, and twenty-five according to others. The connection of this surah to what precedes it is known from what we quoted earlier from al-Jalal al-Suyuti. Some have briefly explained the reason for the order of these three surahs, saying: In Surah al-Infitar there is the description of the recording angels (al-hafazah al-katibin), in Surah al-Mutaffifin is the place where their books are kept, and in this surah is their presentation on the Day of Resurrection.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿When the sky is split asunder﴾, that is, with the clouds, as narrated from Ibn Abbas, and as al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj held, as in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit). The words of the Exalted support this: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open with clouds﴾, so the Qur'an explains one part of it by another. It is also said that it splits due to the terror of the Day of Resurrection, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the sky will be split open, for that Day it will be frail﴾. It has been argued against this that there is no contradiction in the splitting being with clouds.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that it will split from the Milky Way (al-majarrah).

In the reports it is said that it is the gate of the sky. The astronomers (ahl al-hay'ah) say that it is a multitude of small stars, very close together, not distinguished in brightness, and this appears clearly to one who looks at it through observation. There is no contradiction, according to what has been said, between this and the meaning of it being the gate of the sky, namely that the descent and ascent of the angels, peace be upon them, is from its direction; this is due to the common feature that it consists of small stars, close together, not distinguished in brightness.

As for the report: "The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent Mu'adh to the people of Yemen and said to him: 'O Mu'adh, they will ask you about the Milky Way, so say: it is the saliva of a serpent under the Throne.'"

From this it is said that it lies in the frozen sea (al-bahr al-makfuf) beneath the sky, which hardly is sound. The aforementioned view should not be related except to make clear its status. 'Ubayd ibn 'Aqil narrated from Abu 'Amr: "inshaqqat" and likewise the similar words after it, with ishmam of the ta' (kasr-tinged) in pause. Abu 'Ubayd Allah ibn Khalawayh also transmitted from him the kasra, and that is said to be the dialect of Tayy. It is narrated from Abu Hatim: I heard an eloquent Bedouin in the lands of Qays pronounce this ta' (the feminine ta' attached to the verb) with a kasra; and this is a dialect. Perhaps this is because the fawasil (verse-endings) are treated like rhyme (qawafi), so just as this ta' is pronounced with a kasra in rhyme, as in the words of Kuthayyir 'Azzah from a qasidah:

"I am not one who calls down ruin upon 'Azzah, nor one who gloats if it is said 'Azzah has been humbled."

and in other verses of that qasidah it is pronounced with a kasra in the verse-endings. Treating verse-endings in pause like rhyme is a well-known practice, as in His saying, Exalted is He, "al-zununa" and "al-rasula" in Surah al-Ahzab, and assimilating the continuous reading to the state of pause is also found in verse-endings.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verse 2:

﴿And it listened to its Lord﴾, that is, it gave ear to Him, the Exalted. It is said: adhina (to give ear) means "he listened." The poet says:

Deaf when they hear of something good, but when I am mentioned to them with evil, they give ear.

And Qu'nab says:

If they give ear to a suspicion, they fly with it in joy, *** and if they give ear to something righteous, they bury it.

Here, "listening" is a metaphor for submission and obedience; that is, it submitted to the effect of His power, glorified and majestic, when His will, glorified be He, became attached to its splitting, in the manner of an obedient subordinate who submits when the command of the obeyed commander reaches him. The mention of the title "Lord" together with its attribution to it (the heaven) is to signal the cause of the ruling. This sentence and its counterpart after "qil" (it is said) are in the position of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We came willingly﴾ (41:11), in informing that what is attributed to the heaven and the earth of splitting, extension and other things proceeds in accordance with the requirement of wisdom, as they have established.

﴿And it has the right to do so﴾, that is: it was made truly deserving of listening and submission. Yet there is no impossibility in the notion that it was not so, but rather in its very self and essence, from the expression "he is entitled to such-and-such" (mahquq bi-kadha) and "he is worthy of it" (haqiq bihi). The sum of the meaning: it submitted to its Lord, and it is truly and fittingly deserving of submission, because the divine power is not thwarted by any matter among matters, not for a reason that particularly belongs to it out of the possible things. Some have mentioned that the original sense of the expression is "the right of God, exalted, is upon it by that," that is: a ruling was issued upon it that submission is inescapable, in a sense that He, glorified be He, intended from it as an irrevocable will. It was also said: the meaning is: "and it is right for it to split because of the severity of the terror." The sentence, according to what some of the eminent scholars chose, is a parenthetical clause confirming what precedes it; and it was said: it is conjoined to it, but that is not the case.

ِAnd when the earth is stretched out (﴿وإذا الأرْضُ مُدَّتْ﴾). Al-Dahhak said: it is spread out by the leveling of its mountains and hills and their flattening, so it becomes a level plain (qa'an safsafan), in which you will see no crookedness (iwaj) or elevation (amt). Some of them said: it is increased in extent and expansiveness, from "madda-hu" in the sense of "amadda-hu," i.e., increased it; and similar to this is what has been said: it flows, so its expanse increases and its vastness grows.

Al-Hakim related with a good chain of transmission from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The earth will be stretched on the Day of Resurrection like the stretching of a hide (adim), and then there will be for the son of Adam of it only the place of his two feet."

﴿And it casts out what is within it﴾: that is, it throws out what is in its belly of the dead and the treasures. This is the view reported by ʿAbd al-Razzaq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd from Qatadah, and al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'an scholar) also held it. Some scholars, such as Ibn Jubayr and a group with him, limited it to the dead, on the basis that the casting out of treasures happens when the Dajjal (the Antichrist) emerges. It seems that those who hold the first view do not accept that treasures are cast out on that day. Even if they accept it, they may say that it need not be general to all treasures, and that it only happens in this way on the Day of Resurrection. The claim that the Day of Resurrection is broad enough to include the time of the Dajjal's emergence should be set aside and not taken into account.

﴿And it is emptied﴾: that is, it is emptied of what is within it to the utmost degree, until nothing of that remains in it, as if it has exerted its greatest effort in this. The form tafaʿʿala (تفعّل), used here as تَخَلَّتْ, indicates exertion (التكلف), and its purpose is emphasis (المبالغة), as in your saying تحلّم الحليم (the forbearing one feigned forbearance) and تكرّم الكريم (the generous one showed generosity). It has also been said that "it is emptied" means emptied of the living beings upon it, and it has been said that it means emptied of its mountains and seas. Both views, as you see, are weak.

Abu al-Qasim al-Ḥubayli reported in al-Dībāj, from Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am the first whom the earth will split open for. I will sit up in my grave, and the earth will be shaken with me. I will say to it: 'What is the matter with you?' It will say: 'My Lord has commanded me to cast out what is in my belly and to empty myself, so that I become as I was when there was nothing in me.'"

That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it casts out what is within it and is emptied﴾ ﴿and it hearkens to its Lord﴾ in the casting out and what follows it, ﴿and is made to obey﴾. The discussion here is similar to what preceded. It contains an indication that what is mentioned, although it is attributed to the earth, is by the act and power of God, mighty and majestic. The repetition of the word (إذا) "idhā" ("when") is to make each of the two clauses independent, with a kind of power of its own.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verse 6:

﴿Yā ayyuhā al-insānu innaka kādiḥun﴾ means: striving and exerting yourself greatly in your deeds, whether good or evil. ﴿Ilā rabbika kadḥan﴾ means: throughout your life, toward the meeting with your Lord, that is, toward death and what follows it of the states represented by "meeting" and "kadh" (the exertion of the self in work until it leaves its mark on it), from kadaḥa jildahu, when he scratched his skin. Ibn Maqil said:

*"Time is but two turns: in one of them I die, and in the other I seek life, striving."*

And another said:

*"The cheerfulness of every good life has passed away, and I remain striving for life and toiling."*

﴿Fa-mulāqīhi﴾ means: so you will certainly meet Him immediately after that, with nothing to turn you away from Him. The pronoun refers to Him, glorified and exalted; that is, you will meet the recompense of Him, exalted is He. It was also said that it refers to the kadh, meaning you will meet the recompense of the kadh, and this is an intensification of expression, like the saying "Indeed, these are only your deeds returned to you" [*innamā hiya a'mālukum taridu ilaykum*].

[p. 80]

It is apparent that "mulāqīhi" is conjoined to "kādiḥun" on both views. Ibn 'Atiyya, after mentioning the second view, said: "Then *fa-alqāhu* on this reading joins the whole sentence to the sentence before it, and the sense is: *fa-anta mulāqīhi* (so you are one who meets it). The specification does not appear clearly." The intended meaning of "al-insān" is the species, as the division that follows indicates. Muqatil said: the intended one is al-Aswad ibn Hilal al-Makhzumi, who argued with his brother Abu Salama about the matter of resurrection. Abu Salama said: "Yes, by Him who created you, you will certainly ride the layers and you will certainly come to the steep path." Al-Aswad said: "Then where are the earth and the sky, and what is the condition of the people?" It seems he meant that the verse was revealed concerning him, while it encompasses the whole species. It was also said: the intended one is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who was striving in pursuit of this world, harming the Messenger (ﷺ), and persisting in disbelief. Perhaps the speaker also meant this. As for one who went to the extreme of far-fetchedness and held that it refers to the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, the meaning would be: you strive in conveying the messages of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and in guiding His servants, glorified is He, and in bearing harm from the disbelievers. So rejoice that you will meet Allah, exalted is He, with this deed, and it is not lost with Him, may His majesty be exalted.

The response of "idhā" was said to be:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ ﴿he will be judged with an easy reckoning﴾ and so on, is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If there comes to you guidance from Me, then whoever follows My guidance, no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O mankind﴾ and so on is an *i'tiraḍ* (a parenthetical interjection). It was also said that the answer (*jawāb*) is omitted for magnification (*li-l-tahwīl*), meaning: whatever occurred, of a kind that the scope of explanation cannot contain. Some scholars estimated it to be like what is stated in the surahs of al-Takwir and al-Infitar. It was also said that the omitted answer is what is indicated by ﴿O mankind﴾ and so on, its estimate being: ﴿mankind will meet his toil﴾. It was also said that it is that same verse, with the *fa* (then) omitted, the original being: "Then O mankind," or by estimating: "It is said."

Al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad said: it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then you will meet it﴾, with the estimate: "Then you are meeting it," so that together with the estimated element it forms a single sentence. On this view, the sentence ﴿O mankind﴾ and so on is a parenthetical interjection. Ibn al-Anbari and al-Balkhi said: it is (*wa-adhinat*, "and it hearkened") with the *waw* being extra, as was said concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾. On the view of al-Akhfash, the *idhā* here has no answer, because it is not conditional. Rather, in ﴿when the sky is split open﴾ and ﴿when the earth is stretched out﴾, the *idhā* is stripped of conditional force: the *idhā* of "when the sky" is a subject (*mubtada'*), and in "and when the earth" the predicate (*khabar*) is the *waw*, which is extra. The meaning is: at the time the sky is split open, at the time the earth is stretched out. It was also said: it has no answer, because it is not of that kind, but is stripped of the conditional sense and is an object (*maf'ūl*) of an omitted *udhkur* ("remember"). The weakness of some of these views is not hidden. Perhaps the best of them are the first two.

The easy reckoning is the light, facile account in which there is no close scrutiny (*munāqashah*), as was said. The upon him be blessings and peace (ﷺ) explained it as presentation (*'arḍ*) and as looking into the record together with overlooking.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud related on the authority of 'A'isha that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No one is called to account but that he is destroyed." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, may Allah make me your ransom, does Allah not say: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ ﴿he will be judged with an easy reckoning﴾?" He said: "That is only the presentation. They are presented, and whoever is scrutinized in the reckoning is destroyed."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related on the authority of 'A'isha, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say in some of his prayers: 'O Allah, account me with an easy reckoning.' When he had finished, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the easy reckoning?' He said: 'That he looks into his record and He overlooks it for him.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verse 9:

﴿And he will return to his family, joyful.﴾ That is: to his kinsfolk among the believers, delighted with his condition, saying: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ It has also been said: that is, to the company of believers in general, even if they are not his kinsfolk; for all the believers are a "family" (ahl) to the believer by virtue of sharing in faith. It has also been said: that is, to his close associates and to those whom God the Exalted has prepared for him in Paradise, of the houris and the youths; this was narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from Mujahid. And Zayd ibn 'Ali recited: «wa-yuqlabu» (and he will be turned), the imperfect of qulliba (passive voice).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verse 10:

﴿But as for him who is given his record behind his back﴾ means: he is given it in his left hand from behind his back. It has been said: his right hand is chained to his neck and his left hand is placed behind his back, so he is given his record with his left hand. It has also been narrated that his left hand enters his chest until it comes out from behind his back, and he takes his record with it. There is therefore no contradiction between what is mentioned here and what is in Surah al-Haqqah, where the back is not mentioned. Then, this (verse) refers to the disbelievers, while what precedes it refers to the believing God-fearing people. So there is no reference here to the disobedient believers, as al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan) inclines to conclude. It has been said: there is no remoteness in including the disobedient among the People of the Right. Either because they are given their books in the right hand after they leave the Fire, as Ibn 'Atiyyah chose,
[Page 81]
or because they are given them in the right hand before that, but with a reckoning that is greater than the reckoning of the God-fearing and less than the reckoning of the disbelievers. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So he will be called to a light reckoning﴾ would then be a description of all of them by a description of some of them. It has also been said: they are given them in the left hand, and the distinction of the disbelievers lies in the giving being from behind their backs. Perhaps this is because those who are given their books cannot bear to see their faces, due to the utter ugliness of them, or due to the extreme of their hatred for them, or because they cast the Book of God behind their backs.

﴿So he will call out for destruction﴾: he will seek it, call out to it, and say, "Woe to me, O destruction!" Then it will be said, "This is your time." Thubur means ruin, and it encompasses all kinds of hardship. ﴿And he will burn in a blaze﴾: he will suffer its heat, or he will enter it.

Most of the Seven Readers (al-Qurra' al-Sab'a, the seven canonical reciters), along with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Abu al-Shaʿthaʾ, al-Hasan, and al-Aʿraj, recited ﴿yuṣallā﴾ with a damma on the yaʾ, a fatha on the ṣad, and a shadda on the lam, from al-taṣliyah (causing to burn), based on His saying, ﴿and the burning of Hellfire﴾.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verses 13–14:**

﴿Indeed, he was among his family﴾ in the worldly life ﴿joyful﴾, exultant, insolent, pampered, not letting the affairs of the Hereafter occur to his mind, nor reflecting on the outcomes, and he was not sorrowful, reflecting on his state and his end, as is the way of the righteous and the God-fearing. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the cause of what precedes it.

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, he thought that he would never return﴾ is a causal explanation of his joy in the worldly life; that is, he thought he would never return to God, Exalted is He, denying the resurrection (al-ma'ad). It has also been said: he thought he would never return to nothingness; that is, he thought that he would not die, and he was heedless of death, not preparing for it. And that is not correct. The word al-hawr means return in general, and from it is the saying of the poet:

And a man is but like a shooting star, whose light
Returns to ashes after it was blazing.

The restriction here is by the context (qarinat al-maqam). And "an" (أنْ) is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form, and it, together with what follows it in its scope, stands in place of the two objects of the verb of thinking (zann), according to the well-known view.

The restriction here is by the context (qarinat al-maqam). And "an" (أنْ) is the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form, and it, together with what follows it in its scope, stands in place of the two objects of the verb of thinking (zann), according to the well-known view.

Yes [indeed, he will return]: an affirmation of what follows "lan" (never). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, his Lord was ever Seeing of him﴾ is a confirmation and a justification of it. That is: Yes, he will certainly return, for his Lord, mighty and majestic, who created him, has always been seeing of him and of his deeds that necessitate recompense, to such an extent that nothing of them is hidden from Him, glory be to Him. Therefore there must be a return, a reckoning, and a requital.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verse 16:**

﴿So I swear not by the twilight﴾. It is the redness that is seen on the horizon of the west after sunset. Its root is the thinness of a thing. It is said: "shay'un shafaq" (شَيْءٌ شَفَقٌ), meaning a thing that does not hold together because of its thinness. From the same root comes "ashfaqa 'alayhi" (أشْفَقَ عَلَيْهِ), meaning "his heart grew tender toward him." "Al-shafaqah" (الشَّفَقَةُ) is from "al-ishfaq" (الإشْفاق), and likewise "al-shafaq" (الشَّفَقُ). The poet said:

"She loves my life, and I love its death out of tenderness, and death is the most generous guest to alight upon the noble."

It is also said that it is the whiteness that follows that redness and is seen after it disappears. There is a difference of opinion over calling that whiteness "shafaq." The majority hold that it is not called by this name. Abu Hurayra, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with them all, hold that it is called by this name. Asad ibn Amr narrated from Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, that he retracted this view in favour of the position of the majority. The full discussion of this is in the commentaries on al-Hidaya (a classical work of Hanafi jurisprudence).

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid and Ikrima that it here refers to the whole day. This is also reported from al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi Najih. It seems that what encouraged them to this view is that the night is mentioned after it by conjunction. From Ikrima also comes the view that it refers to what remains of the day.

The "fa" (الفاء) in "fa-la" (فَلا) answers an implied conditional clause. The meaning is: "If you have understood this, or you have confirmed the return to life through resurrection, then I do not swear by the twilight."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verse 17:**

﴿And the night and what it gathers together (wasaqa)﴾: that is, what it gathers and collects. It is said: "wasaqahu, fa-ttasaqa and istawsaqa," meaning he gathered it and it became gathered together. It is also said: "ta'amun mawsuq," meaning gathered; and "ibilun mustawsaqa," meaning congregated. The poet said:

*Indeed we have she-camels, noble and pure, gathering together, which have found no driver.*

Among the derivatives of *wasq* (a load, a measure) are the gathered "asw'a" (sing. sa'), which are sixty sa's, or a camel's load, because of its being gathered on its back. The *ma* in ﴿وما وسَقَ﴾ may be either a verbal (masdariyya) or a relative (mawsula) particle. The majority hold the second view, and the returning pronoun is omitted; that is, "and He who gathers it (wasaqahu)." What is meant by it is what gathers at night and returns to its place of rest among animals and others.
Page 82
From Mujahid: what there is in it of good or evil. It was also said: what it covers and conceals with its darkness. It was also said: what it gathers of darkness. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jubayr that he said: ﴿وما وسَقَ﴾ "and what it works upon (ʿamila fihi)." From this is his saying:

*One day you see us righteous, and at another time it makes us rise like one who girds up and is ready to go.*

It was also said: *wasaqa* here means "drove"; that is, what it drove to its places among animals and others, or what it drove away of daylight's light. From this is *al-wasiqa*, which in the Qamus he described as: among camels, like a company of people; when they are stolen, they are driven off together.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verses 18–19:**

﴿Wa-l-qamari idha ittasaqa﴾ — that is, when its light gathers and it becomes full (badr).

﴿Latarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq﴾ — this is an address to the species of mankind, which was called first, in consideration of its encompassing its individuals. By "riding" (rukub) is meant encountering (mula'ah). The tabaq (layer, stage) originally means anything that corresponds to something else in every respect, and in common usage it is specialized to a state that corresponds to another state. From this is the verse of al-Aqra' ibn Habis:

*InnI imru'un qad halabtu l-dahra ashtarahu / wa-sani'ni tabaqun minhu ila tabaq*

"Indeed I am a man who has milked time to its last portions, and a stage of it has driven me from one stage to another."

The "'an" here indicates passing beyond (mujawaza). Many commentators said it means "ba'da" (after), as in the words of the two: *sadu-ka kabiran 'an kabir* ("they succeeded you, elder after elder"), and the verse:

*Ma ziltu aqta'u manhalan 'an manhal / hatta anakhtu bi-bab 'Abd al-Wahid*

"I have not ceased crossing one watering place after another until I made camp at the gate of 'Abd al-Wahid."

Passing beyond and succession (ba'diyya) are close in meaning. The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element which occurs as an adjective to "tabaqan" or as a circumstantial (hal) from the subject of "latarkabunna." The apparent view is that "tabaqan" is in the accusative as a direct object; that is, *latulaqunna* (you will surely encounter) a state passing beyond another state, or existing after a state, or passing beyond states, or existing after states, each one corresponding to its sister in severity and terror. It is also permitted that "rukub" be in its literal sense, with the state made "markuba" (ridden) figuratively. It has been said that the accusative of "tabaqan" is by analogy with an adverbial of place or time, or is circumstantial. A group said: "tabaq" is the plural of "tabaqa," like *tukhamun* and *tukhama*, meaning rank or level. It is said it is a collective noun whose singular is that (tabaqa). The meaning: you will surely ride states after states, which are levels in severity, some higher than others, namely death and what follows it of the stations of the Resurrection and its terrors. Al-Tibi preferred this, saying: "This is what the structure requires, and the sequence of the fa' in *fa-la uqsimu* upon the saying of the Exalted: *bala inna rabbahu kana bihi basiran*" ("Nay, indeed His Lord is ever seeing of him"). Some interpreted the states as what occurs in this world from being a drop of semen until death, and what occurs in the Hereafter from resurrection until the time of settling in one of the two abodes. It has been said: it is possible that "tabaqan 'an tabaq" means the death corresponding to the original non-existence and the revival corresponding to the previous revival, so the speech is an oath upon resurrection after death, and what al-Tibi mentioned applies to it.

Nu'aym ibn Hammad and Abu Nu'aym related from Makhul that he said regarding the verse: "In every twenty years you will be in a state you were not in like it." In the narration of Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim from him: "Every twenty years you will produce a matter you were not upon." So "tabaq" means twenty years, and this has been counted in the Qamus among its meanings, and what was mentioned is an explanation of the intended meaning. It has been said:

"Tabaq" here means a generation (qarn) of people, like it in the words of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib praising the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

*Wa-anta lamma wulidta ashraqati l-ard / wa-da'at bi-nurika l-ufuq*
"When you were born, the earth shone and the horizon brightened with your light."

*Tanaqqala min salbin ila rahimin / idha mada 'alamun bada tabaq*
"You moved from loin to womb, and when one world passed, a generation appeared."

And the meaning is: you will surely follow the ways of those who passed before you, generation after generation. Both of these views go against the apparent sense.

Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Aswad, Ibn Jubayr, Masruq, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-'Aliya, Ibn Thabbat, Talha, 'Isa, the two brothers (al-Akhawan), and Ibn Kathir read: "latarkabunna" with the second-person address (ta' of address) and a fatha on the ba'. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud that they also kasra'd the ta' of the imperfect, which is the dialect of Banu Tamim, on the basis that it is also an address to mankind, but in consideration of the wording and not of the encompassing. Al-Bukhari related from Ibn 'Abbas that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this was narrated from a group. It seems that whoever holds that he (ﷺ) is the one meant by "al-insan" in what preceded goes this way, and on this reading the meaning is: "you will ride noble states after another [state of] nearness in degrees, or degrees of severity in this world, in consideration of what he (ﷺ) suffers from the disbelievers and endures in conveying the message," or the speech is a promise of victory: you will surely encounter conquest after conquest, and victory after victory, and glad tidings of the Ascension (mi'raj); that is, you will surely ride heaven after heaven, as 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. This is supported by the emphasis with the oath-clause and the sequence with the denial-clause.

Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said regarding this, meaning: "the sky splits, then cracks, then turns red." In another narration: "the sky becomes like molten brass, and becomes like red oil-dregs, and becomes weak, and splits, so it becomes state after state." Thus the "ta'" is for the feminine, and the implied subject refers to the sky. Umar and Ibn 'Abbas also read: "layarkabunna" with the ya' of the third person and a fatha on the ba', by way of iltifat (shift) from addressing mankind to the third person. And from Ibn 'Abbas: meaning "your Prophet" (ﷺ), so the pronoun is for him (ﷺ), and the meaning is as previously stated. It has been said: the implied third-person pronoun refers to the moon, because it changes in states from crescent, to new moon, to full moon. Umar also read: "liyurkabunna" with the ya' of the third person and a damma on the ba', with the plural pronoun referring to mankind in consideration of encompassing. It was also read with the ta' of the second person and a kasra on the ba', on the feminine address of mankind in consideration of the self. The matter of the implied circumstantial (al-haliyya) indicated earlier is not hidden under these readings.

The fa' in His saying, ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ may be taken as indicating that what follows, the denial and expression of wonder, is a consequence of what precedes it: the states and terrors of the Day of Resurrection, referred to by His saying ﴿You will surely ride﴾ and so on, which in some respects necessitate faith and prostration. That is: if their condition on the Day of Resurrection is as has been indicated, then what is wrong with them, being unbelievers? That is, what prevents them from believing in Allah the Exalted, His Messenger (ﷺ), and all else that must be believed in, especially when its necessitating factors, the terrors which will befall whoever abandons it on that day, converge?

It may also be taken that this is a consequence of what is said about the great status of the Prophet (ﷺ), referred to by His saying, glorified is He, ﴿You will surely ride﴾ and so on, in respect of another of the aspects previously mentioned concerning it. That is: if his (ﷺ) state and status are as has been indicated, then what prevents them from believing in him (ﷺ)?

It may further be taken that this is a consequence of what His saying, glorified is He, ﴿So I swear﴾ and so on includes, of things that indicate the validity of resurrection, namely the heavenly and earthly transformations which show complete power. This is the view of the Imam (al-Razi). That is: if His state, exalted is His state, is as has been indicated, of His being glorified and exalted, of great power and vast knowledge, then what prevents them from believing in the resurrection, which is among the possible things that His power, mighty and majestic, encompasses and His knowledge, glorious in majesty, comprehends?

The verse ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾ is coordinated with the preceding circumstantial clause, so it is also circumstantial (ḥāliyyah) like it. The meaning is: what prevents them from prostrating when the Qur'an is recited? The word "sujūd" (prostration) is metaphorical for the submission (khuḍūʿ) that is necessarily entailed, as narrated from Qatadah. Alternatively, it may mean prayer (ṣalāh). Pairing this with faith (īmān) indicates the great status of prayer, as is well known. Or the word may be taken in its literal sense. What precedes it, "the Qur'an is recited," refers to the recitation of the Qur'an in general, or to the recitation containing a verse of prostration.

It is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he prostrated when reciting this verse.

Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We prostrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord﴾."

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Rafi', who said: "I prayed the ʿAtamah (the night prayer) with Abu Hurayrah, and he recited ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and prostrated. I asked him about it, and he said: 'I prostrated behind Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ), and I will not cease prostrating in it until I meet him (ﷺ).'"

This is a refutation of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "There is no prostration in the mufaṣṣal (the final portion of the Qur'an), and it is from the surah of Muhammad (ﷺ)." It was also said: [it is] from al-Fath (Surah 48). And it was said that the view of most scholars is that there is a prostration in al-Ḥujurāt. The prostration is recommended (sunnah) according to al-Shafiʿi and obligatory according to Abu Hanifah.

The Imam said: It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited one day ﴿Prostrate and draw near﴾, and he prostrated, and those believers with him prostrated, while the Quraysh were clapping above their heads and whistling. Then this verse was revealed.

Abu Hanifah argued for the obligation of the prostration from this in two respects:

The first: that the Prophet's action (ﷺ) requires obligation, due to His saying (Exalted is He): (follow him).

The second: that He (Exalted is He) censured those who hear it and do not prostrate, and the occurrence of censure upon omission indicates obligation. End of quotation.

There is a discussion on this, and also Ibn Hajar said that the hadith is not established.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verse 22:

﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve deny﴾ i.e., the Qur'an. This is a shift from their not prostrating when it is recited to their openly denying it. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is placed in the position of their pronoun in order to brand them with disbelief and to indicate the reason for the ruling. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Abla read: «yakdhibun» with the letter ya' vowelled with a fatha and the dhal unstressed (i.e., yakdhibūn, from the unstressed form).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 84, verse 23:

﴿And Allah is most knowing of what they harbour﴾ That is: of what they conceal in their breasts of disbelief, envy, hatred and transgression. Here "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), and its returning pronoun (al-ʾāʾid) is omitted. The original sense of al-iʿāʾ (إيعاء, "storing") is placing a thing into a container (wiʿāʾ). In al-Rāghib's Mufradāt: al-iʿāʾ is the keeping of goods in a container, and from it is his saying:

"The worst of what you have stored up as provision is evil."

Here it is used figuratively to mean concealment (al-iḍmār), and this is what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. It does not follow from this that the verse concerns the hypocrites, even though the surah is Meccan, as is not hidden. Some commentators interpreted it as "gathering" (al-jamʿ), and this is related from Ibn Zayd. It is also permissible that the meaning is: "And Allah is most knowing of what they gather in their records of evil deeds." In any case, Allah's knowledge of this is a metaphor (kināyah) for His recompense for it, glorified is He. It has been said: the purpose is to indicate that behind their denial there are great and numerous abominations whose description the scope of expression cannot contain. Some have said: it may be that the meaning is: "And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal within themselves of the proofs that it, i.e., the Qur'an, is true," so the purpose is exaggeration of their obstinacy and their denial contrary to their knowledge. The apparent reading is that, on this view, the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿they deny﴾. Its being so on what has been said regarding indication is contrary to the apparent meaning. Abu Raja' read: "bi-mā yaʿūna," from waʿā, yaʿī.

The verse "So give them tidings of a painful punishment" (﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾) is connected to the preceding report of His knowledge, may He be exalted, of what they hoard (﴿بِما يُوعُونَ﴾), with the meaning that He will recompense them for it. It is also said that it is connected to their denial. It is further said that the *fa'* is *fasiha* (an elliptical "fa" that signals an implied condition), meaning: since their state is what has been mentioned, then give them tidings, etc. ... Tabshir (giving good news) in its common usage means informing of something pleasant, and the use of the term here is in the manner of the line of poetry:

*"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."*

It is also permitted that this is by way of treating them, because of their immersion in sins that necessitate punishment and their failure to refrain from them, as though they were eager for the punishment, so that informing them of it is like giving glad tidings and informing them of something pleasant. The difference between the two interpretations becomes apparent upon slight reflection. Far more remote is the view of the one who said that this is an allusion to the Prophet of Mercy (ﷺ) being loved for bringing glad tidings, so that the word "tabshir" is used metaphorically for his task of warning, in order to console his heart (ﷺ).

Except those who believe and do righteous deeds. This is an exception of the disconnected kind (al-istithna' al-munqati', an exception that does not belong to the same category as what precedes it) from the pronoun in the accusative case in ﴿so give them good news﴾. It is also permissible for it to be a connected exception (al-istithna' al-muttasil), with the excepted group understood as those among them who believed and did righteous deeds afterward, meaning from among those disbelievers. The past tense in the two verbs is then understood in view of God's knowledge, or both verbs carry the meaning of the present tense. The difficulty in this is not hidden, and the first reading is more suitable than it, given God's words: ﴿for them is a reward that will never end﴾. This is because the reward mentioned is not restricted to the believers among them but applies to all believers. That the restriction is relative, applying only in comparison with those among them who remained in disbelief, goes against the apparent meaning. Moreover, the implication of restriction to the believers among them is sufficient for the purpose, as is not hidden.

The tanwin (nunation) in ﴿ajrun﴾ ("a reward") is for glorification (lil-ta'zim). The meaning of ﴿ghayru mamnun﴾ ("never ending") is: not cut off, from the verb "manna" (to cut) when it is cut off; or: not counted as a favor and not reckoned against them, from "manna 'alayhi" (to bestow a favor upon someone with reproach) when one counts a kindness and reckons it as a debt. Some scholars took "mann" in this sense to derive also from "manna" meaning "to cut", because it cuts off the blessing and requires the cutting off of its gratitude. The clause, according to what has been said, is a resumptive statement (isti'naf muqarrir) confirming what the exception indicates, namely the removal of punishment from those mentioned, and it explains the manner of this and its accompaniment with the great and abundant reward.
